newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leaner, meaner Daimler seen emerging from overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Leaner, meaner Daimler seen emerging from overhaul.

text.p: German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG will emerge as a leaner, more profitable company after announcing restructuring plans that will legally wind up its Mercedes-Benz cars unit, analysts said on Friday.

In a statement that is to be formally approved next week, Daimler said late on Thursday that it plans to merge its Mercedes-Benz unit into the group structure and slash layers of middle and upper management.

Although the legal end of Mercedes was accompanied by the resignation its highly-respected chairman Helmut Werner, analysts said the Daimler overhaul was long overdue. It is a step toward speeding what has been a notoriously cumbersome management structure, they added.
"The overall management structure is much leaner," said Lothar Lubinetski, analyst at Enskilda Corporate. "That should be very positive for Daimler."
Maybe the only question mark hanging over the reorganisation is the future direction of Mercedes itself but most analysts expected little change.
Whereas Werner had spent almost his entire career in the automotive industry, Schrempp climbed the corporate ladder at Daimler-Benz Aerospace.

Some analysts fear that Schrempp may try to exert greater control over the car business, especially since he was thought not be fully behind Werner's strategy of widening Mercedes' fleet into smaller and sportier cars.

A majority of experts, however, said that with Werner's strategy already starting to bear fruit with new models such as the SLK selling better than expected, Schrempp will likely stay the present course.
"Schrempp and Werner could not remain at the company at the same time," said Rolla Kautz, analyst at BHF-Trust. "But the positive trend for the car business at Mercedes is assured."
Under the overhaul, Mercedes will cease to be a legal company and will be represented by three executives on the Daimler board, one for cars, one for trucks and one for advertising.

The group's other two major units, Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) and financial services and information technology company Debis AG will remain legal entitities. But the company is expected to cut out a management layer at DASA, giving it the same number as Debis.

Analysts said the overhaul will be costly at first, with Daimler forced to compensate staff that will be laid off. But that the move will eventually yield cost savings in the low hundreds of millions of marks a year.

Hans Hartmann, analyst at Dresdner International Advisers said that history has shown that companies with an operational management structure are normally more successful than financial holding structures such as those at Daimler up to now.
"The new management structure should be more efficient," he said.

But maybe more important for Daimler will be a more nimble decision-making process. Daimler sources said that under the current structure it can sometimes take months for relatively simple matters such as a factory budget to be finally approved.
Analysts said that Daimler's 23 operating units, now more closely under the scrutiny of the board, will be put under more pressure to increase profits.
Each unit is expected to produce its own profit and loss statement and live up to Daimler's goal of achieving a 12 percent return on capital employed.
"There is going to be more pressure on management," Lubinetski said. "That is very good."
Although unrelated to Thursday's announcement, analysts expect the number of units to be trimmed still further to around 20 different operations.
